questions.question: A firewall admin must permit only secure, TLS-encrypted web browsing out while plain HTTP on port 80 stays blocked. Which destination port do they open?
questions.explanation: HTTPS rides TLS on TCP port 443; port 80 is unencrypted HTTP.

questions.question: A host knows its gateway's IP is 192.168.1.1 but must learn the gateway's MAC to build an Ethernet frame, so it broadcasts 'who has 192.168.1.1?' Which protocol resolves this?
questions.explanation: ARP maps IPv4 addresses to MAC addresses via broadcast requests on the LAN.

questions.question: An admin configures a /24 network so roughly 250 hosts share one flat subnet. Write that prefix's mask in dotted-decimal notation.
A live-streaming app drops an occasional frame but never stalls to retransmit, because its transport sends datagrams with no handshake or ordering guarantees. Which protocol is it using?
questions.explanation: UDP is connectionless with no retransmission — low latency at the cost of reliability.

questions.question: A developer tests a web server running on their own machine; traffic never reaches the network card because the address refers to the local host itself. Which IPv4 address do they ping?
questions.explanation: 127.0.0.1 is the IPv4 loopback — traffic to it never leaves the host.

questions.question: A laptop joins Wi-Fi and instantly receives an IP address, subnet mask, gateway, and DNS server as a timed lease with no manual entry. Which protocol supplied that configuration?
questions.explanation: DHCP automatically leases addressing information to hosts joining a network.

questions.question: Servers in three datacenters must agree on time within milliseconds so their logs can be correlated. Which standard protocol synchronizes their clocks?
questions.explanation: NTP synchronizes computer clocks over the network to millisecond accuracy.

questions.question: An admin opens an encrypted remote shell to a Linux server over untrusted hotel Wi-Fi so credentials and commands can't be sniffed the way Telnet allows. Which protocol is used?
questions.explanation: SSH provides encrypted remote login, replacing plaintext Telnet.

questions.question: Thirty home devices with 192.168.x.x addresses share one public IP because the router rewrites source addresses and ports on outbound packets. Which technology is this?
questions.explanation: NAT translates private addresses to the router's public address, multiplexing many hosts.

questions.question: An ISP has exhausted its IPv4 pool and must deploy the successor protocol offering 128-bit hexadecimal addresses like 2001:db8::1. Name it.
questions.explanation: IPv6's 128-bit addresses provide ~3.4 x 10^38 addresses versus IPv4's ~4.3 billion.

questions.question: A network uses the subnet mask 255.255.255.0. How many usable host addresses does each subnet provide?
questions.explanation: The mask leaves 8 host bits = 256 addresses; subtracting the network and broadcast addresses leaves 254 usable.

questions.question: A user can ping 8.8.8.8 successfully, but every website name fails to load. Which service is broken?
questions.explanation: Reaching a raw IP proves connectivity works, so the failure is in translating names to addresses — DNS.

questions.question: A home router holds the public address 203.0.113.5 while a laptop inside the network shows 192.168.1.10. What class is the laptop's address?
questions.explanation: The 192.168.x.x range is reserved for private networks and is translated to the public address by NAT.

questions.question: A traceroute to a website fails at the very first hop. Which LAN device — the one packets must reach first to leave the local network — is likely unreachable?
questions.explanation: The default gateway is the LAN's exit point; a dead first hop means the router itself is not responding.

questions.question: An ISP runs out of IPv4 addresses for new customers. Which headline feature of IPv6 permanently solves this shortage?
questions.explanation: IPv6's 128-bit space provides roughly 3.4 x 10^38 addresses, eliminating the exhaustion of 32-bit IPv4.
